$S=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt[4]{6}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{3}{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}(1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\cdot 2|t|\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{16}{3}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟹{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t=\frac{3}{16}\text{d}u.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt[4]{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $9$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{3}{16}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[(9)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(27-1) \\  & =13\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "08362200-3b6f-52bb-9fff-49cbac1aba34" :step/next {:db/id 17592186530555}} {:db/id 17592186530555 :step/content {:db/id 17592186530493 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c15a0040-721e-5583-80c4-6b4b6d161036" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi(2-\sqrt{3})" :db/id 17592186530062}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186530062} :answer-field/id #uuid "6b596d95-5abf-5a25-8619-bd46ab687c7e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186530300}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "95891d65-20e2-5732-9bd4-e52bbf49b5d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-352088" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{t}{2})),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡(t/2)}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{csc}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{cot}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ | $\frac{\pi }{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1}2\pi \,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[u]}_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1} \\  & =2\pi (1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3a2cc474-bbd9-524c-88cd-2cfdbe4a121b"} {:db/id 17592186530558 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129488 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "276f10df-f807-54a9-b01f-7cf1b357ec66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}t\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186529665} {:answer/id #uuid "8f170c4b-c5f7-5356-8a5a-6fd851ea13ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186529925} {:answer/id #uuid "a53f81c5-8ba3-5b6b-9818-2872dc69946f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}t\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186529990} {:answer/id #uuid "b86bdc8d-5bf9-5ea7-8414-b3dab58e55bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186530042} {:answer/id #uuid "e9f6ac1e-5d34-5fa1-a3ce-c20f5afa43d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186530163}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186529990} :answer-field/id #uuid "4a8fb9e3-9863-5703-95c1-0d8295fc07d3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186126428}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "497a1af7-923f-5a2e-82d5-147a5d2a1d6d" :question/math-academy-id "q-138945" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}t,\,y=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2},\,t\in [0,\sqrt{3}].

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}t)=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2})=\frac{1}{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2}t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}(1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{2}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}t)=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2})=\frac{1}{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2}t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}(1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{2}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[(4)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8d943a17-8038-5310-ba12-619cf9e0f21c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186530550}} {:db/id 17592186530550 :step/content {:db/id 17592186530454 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f3256b67-7e99-5826-a95a-b55a197e4d06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "13\pi" :db/id 17592186530184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186530184} :answer-field/id #uuid "12fa28de-d131-50b4-b0e1-7dd696b0e54f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186530230}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4f72f786-eb31-5b03-9051-ae70858e9f5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-352035" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt[4]{6}.$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{3}{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}(1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\cdot 2|t|\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{cot}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ | $\frac{\pi }{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1}2\pi \,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[u]}_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1} \\  & =2\pi (1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}

"496fa617-6592-57af-89ac-b77d68df0bb3" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Lagrange System With Two Constraints"}] :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y,z) =  x-y-z$ on the intersection of the plane $x+y+z=2$ and the cylinder $x^2+z^2=4.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the minimum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z) =   x-y-z
$$

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x+y+z=2, \qquad h(x,y,z)=x^2 + z^2 = 4.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=2 \\ h(x,y,z) &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩+\mu ⟨2x,0,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=\lambda +2\mu x \\ -1 &=\lambda \\ -1 &=\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{1}{\mu } \\ \lambda &=-1 \\ \mu z &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu$ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction. So, from the third equation above, we must have $z=0.$

Next, we substitute $z=0$  into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $z$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=2$ and $z= 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =2 \\ 2+y+0 & =2 \\ 2+y & =2 \\ y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=-2$ and $z=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =2 \\ -2+y+0 & =2 \\ -2+y & =2 \\ y & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(2, 0, 0), \qquad (-2, 4, 0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(2, 0, 0 )$ | $(-2, 4, 0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $2$ | $-6$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-2, 4, 0),$ and its minimum value is $-6.$"} {:db/id 17592186172382 :question/id #uuid "332ef138-daaa-584b-88e1-280c181c6e29" $$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}3 &=\lambda +8\mu x \\ 2 &=2\lambda +4\mu y \\ 1 &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{1}{4\mu } \\ \mu y &=0 \\ \lambda &=1\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & =1 \\ 4{x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y+z & =1 \\ -\frac{1}{2}+2(0)+z & =1 \\ -\frac{1}{2}+z & =1 \\ z & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
(\frac{1}{2},0,\frac{1}{2}),\,(-\frac{1}{2},0,\frac{3}{2}).

| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $2$ | $0$ |

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=1 \\ h(x,y,z) &=4\end{aligned}\right.

\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨4,1,-1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨0,1,-1⟩+\mu ⟨2x,0,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}4 &=2\mu x \\ 1 &=\lambda \\ -1 &=-\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{2}{\mu } \\ \lambda &=1 \\ \mu z &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-z & =1 \\ y-0 & =1 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute  $z=0$ into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(2,1,0),\,(-2,1,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(2,1,0)$ | $(-2,1,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $9$ | $-7$ |

Constraints"}] :question/problem "Suppose we want to find the minimum of the function $f(x,y,z)=2xz+y^2$ on the intersection of the surfaces $x-z=2$ and $x^2+y^2+2z^2=3$ using the method of Lagrange multipliers. Then, the corresponding Lagrange multipliers $\lambda$ and $\mu$ satisfy the following system: 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}⟨2z,\,\bbox[2pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}},\,2x⟩ &=\lambda ⟨1,\,0,\,\bbox[2pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}}\,⟩+\mu ⟨2x,\,2y,\,\bbox[2pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}}\,⟩ \\ x-z &=2 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the expressions?" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the minimum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z) = 2xz+y^2
$$

 

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x-z=2, \qquad h(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2+2z^2=3.
$$

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=2 \\ h(x,y,z) &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We now expand the first equation of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨2z,\,2y,\,2x⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩+\mu ⟨2x,\,2y,\,4z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

the method of Lagrange multipliers. Then, the corresponding Lagrange multipliers $\lambda $ and $\mu $ satisfy the following system: 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}⟨3,\,\bbox[2pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}},\,2⟩ &=\lambda ⟨2x,\,2y,\,\bbox[2pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}}\,⟩+\mu ⟨4x,\,2y,\,\bbox[2pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}}\,⟩ \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} &=1 \\ 2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the expressions?" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the maximum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z)=3x+2z+{y}^{2}

$$
g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,\,h(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}=1.
$$

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=1 \\ h(x,y,z) &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨3,\,2y,\,2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,\,2y,\,0⟩+\mu ⟨4x,\,2y,\,8z⟩\end{aligned}

3380} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186173090 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173258 :tutorial/content "We can find global extrema of multivariable functions subject to multiple constraints using the method of Lagrange multipliers. 

For example, suppose that we want to find the minimum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z) = 4xy+z^2
$$

subject to the following *two* constraints: 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2=1, \qquad h(x,y,z)=2x^2 + 4y^2 - z = 0
$$

Geometrically, this means that we want to minimize $f(x,y,z)$ over the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and the elliptic paraboloid $2x^2 + 4y^2 - z = 0,$ as shown below.

![](images/0b/0b16f73e034724a9f38d91a606f627db85299507552c45192e91c39bc0c6725a.png)

The method of Lagrange multipliers states that the extrema of the function $f(x,y,z)$ subject to constraints $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b$ can be found by solving the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=a \\ h(x,y,z) &=b\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Here, the constants $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are the Lagrange multipliers of this system.

As before, this method assumes that $\nabla g \neq \mathbf{0}$ and $\nabla h \neq \mathbf{0}$ on the curves $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b,$ and that the extreme values exist.

**Note:** Geometrically, the condition $\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g + \mu \nabla h$ states that

- $\nabla f$ lies in the plane spanned by $\nabla g$ and $\nabla h,$ or, equivalently,

- $\nabla f$ is perpendicular to the level surfaces $g(x,y,z) = a$ and $h(x,y,z) = b.$

We'll explore this geometric intuition further at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "0a4ed8aa-0e0e-50d4-9745-3d68b92cca3a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7745 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} 17592186173091}} {:db/id 17592186173096 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173262 :tutorial/content "Let's now justify why the Lagrange multipliers method works with multiple constraints.

Suppose we wish to optimize the function $f(x,y,z)$ subject to the constraints $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b.$ 

Note the following:

- The natural domain of $f$ is some subset of $\mathbb R^3.$

- If we were to impose the first constraint only, we'd restrict the domain of $f$ to points on the level surface $g(x,y,z)=a.$

- Similarly, if we were to impose the second constraint only, we'd restrict the domain of $f$ to points on the level surface $h(x,y,z)=b.$

- Thus, by imposing *both* constraints, we restrict the domain of $f$ to the *intersection* of these two level surfaces. The intersection of two surfaces is a curve, which we'll denote as $\mathbf r(t)$ for some real parameter $t.$

The curve $\mathbf r(t)$ and the level surfaces are shown below.

![](images/e8/e8b1db73c9952642ba53983ffb7090ad147ae965f1b935a812811742330b4dfc.png)

Now, let $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ be a point that lies on $\mathbf r(t)$ for some $t = t_0$ that is an extrema (max or min) of $f.$

Since $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b$ are level surfaces of the functions $g(x,y,z)$ and $h(x,y,z),$ we have the following:

- $\nabla g$ is perpendicular to $g(x,y,z)=a$ at $P,$ and is therefore perpendicular to $\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$

- $\nabla h$ is perpendicular to $h(x,y,z)=b$ at $P,$ and is therefore perpendicular to $\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$

The situation is sketched below.

![](images/16/16f2f1818628d9eb12ed0f3f2834cd916101839362813afe1be3f90ea35dd104.png)

Let's now compute $\big[f(\mathbf r(t))\big]',$ the derivative of $f$ over the curve $\mathbf r(t).$ By the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[f(r(t))]^{′} & =[f(x(t),y(t),z(t))]^{′} \\  & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\cdot {x}^{′}(t)+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\cdot {y}^{′}(t)+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\cdot {z}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩\cdot ⟨{x}^{′}(t),{y}^{′}(t),{z}^{′}(t)⟩ \\  & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $P$ is an extremum, we must have 

$$
\big[f(\mathbf{r}(t_0))\big]' = 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t_0)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t_0) = 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t_0)) \perp \mathbf{r}'(t_0).
$$

Since $\mathbf{r}'(t_0)$ is tangent to $\mathbf r(t)$ at $P,$ we have that $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t_0))$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$

So, $\nabla g$ and $\nabla h$ are both perpendicular to $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $P$. Assuming they aren't parallel, they span the two-dimensional space perpendicular to $\mathbf{r}(t)$. Now $\nabla f$ is also perpendicular to $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $P$. This means that $\nabla f$ lies in the plane spanned by $\nabla g$ and $\nabla h.$ This condition can be represented by the following equation:

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y,z) + \mu \nabla h(x,y,z),
$$

where the real numbers $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are the Lagrange multipliers.

![](images/b4/b48d7973b28bbd6a99704736dd60737d2f74ebcc2ddfddb0ab6f4749002e826e.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "669fb037-8c12-5658-a176-7753a99e8c7e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7919 :tutorial/title "Justification of the Lagrange Multiplier Method With Multiple Constraints"} :step/id #uuid "db6afef3-511c-5ea5-8a1f-0ce1b0640983" :step/math-academy-id 45619}] :activity/title "Lagrange Multipliers With Multiple Constraints" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172187} {:db/id 17592186173090 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173258 :tutorial/content "We can find global extrema of multivariable functions subject to multiple constraints using the method of Lagrange multipliers.

We'll explore this geometric intuition further at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "0a4ed8aa-0e0e-50d4-9745-3d68b92cca3a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7745 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "bf9461c1-00f3-5778-a2ae-8c56f71f3522" :step/math-academy-id 44838 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173092}} {:db/id 17592186173258 :tutorial/content "We can find global extrema of multivariable functions subject to multiple constraints using the method of Lagrange multipliers. 

For example, suppose that we want to find the minimum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z) = 4xy+z^2
$$

subject to the following *two* constraints: 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2=1, \qquad h(x,y,z)=2x^2 + 4y^2 - z = 0
$$

Geometrically, this means that we want to minimize $f(x,y,z)$ over the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and the elliptic paraboloid $2x^2 + 4y^2 - z = 0,$ as shown below.

![](images/0b/0b16f73e034724a9f38d91a606f627db85299507552c45192e91c39bc0c6725a.png)

The method of Lagrange multipliers states that the extrema of the function $f(x,y,z)$ subject to constraints $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b$ can be found by solving the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=a \\ h(x,y,z) &=b\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Here, the constants $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are the Lagrange multipliers of this system.

As before, this method assumes that $\nabla g \neq \mathbf{0}$ and $\nabla h \neq \mathbf{0}$ on the curves $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b,$ and that the extreme values exist.

**Note:** Geometrically, the condition $\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g + \mu \nabla h$ states that

- $\nabla f$ lies in the plane spanned by $\nabla g$ and $\nabla h,$ or, equivalently,

- $\nabla f$ is perpendicular to the level surfaces $g(x,y,z) = a$ and $h(x,y,z) = b.$

We'll explore this geometric intuition further at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "0a4ed8aa-0e0e-50d4-9745-3d68b92cca3a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7745 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186173092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172135 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171717 :question/id #uuid "b8496dce-3f8b-5516-874d-17d82cfb41b7" :question/math-academy-id "e-12459"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "355c5dfd-d06f-56ef-9c38-8dccf702467e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049390}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172383} {:db/id 17592186172384} {:db/id 17592186363479} {:db/id 17592186363486} {:db/id 17592186363493} {:db/id 17592186401391} {:db/id 17592186401398} {:db/id 17592186493914} {:db/id 17592186493939} {:db/id 17592186493941} {:db/id 17592186512931}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing a Lagrange System With Two Constraints"} :step/id #uuid "6f4656de-85c7-583b-9753-5e82a5f0e76f" :step/math-academy-id 44841 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173091}} {:db/id 17592186173091 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172134 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171716 :question/id #uuid "fbe81109-2a56-5dd3-bab5-4ac5cc6ca860" :question/math-academy-id "e-12458"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "496fa617-6592-57af-89ac-b77d68df0bb3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172382} {:db/id 17592186172385} {:db/id 17592186363500} {:db/id 17592186363507} {:db/id 17592186389367} {:db/id 17592186389374} {:db/id 17592186411873} {:db/id 17592186493923} {:db/id 17592186493936} {:db/id 17592186493964} {:db/id 17592186493972} {:db/id 17592186512883}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Lagrange System With Two Constraints"} :step/id #uuid "3e24f68c-7b46-5dbe-8a10-39bed7e5ffb5" :step/math-academy-id 44839 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173096}} {:db/id 17592186173096 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173262 :tutorial/content "Let's now justify why the Lagrange multipliers method works with multiple constraints.

Suppose we wish to optimize the function $f(x,y,z)$ subject to the constraints $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b.$ 

Note the following:

- The natural domain of $f$ is some subset of $\mathbb R^3.$

- If we were to impose the first constraint only, we'd restrict the domain of $f$ to points on the level surface $g(x,y,z)=a.$

- Similarly, if we were to impose the second constraint only, we'd restrict the domain of $f$ to points on the level surface $h(x,y,z)=b.$

- Thus, by imposing *both* constraints, we restrict the domain of $f$ to the *intersection* of these two level surfaces. The intersection of two surfaces is a curve, which we'll denote as $\mathbf r(t)$ for some real parameter $t.$

The curve $\mathbf r(t)$ and the level surfaces are shown below.

![](images/e8/e8b1db73c9952642ba53983ffb7090ad147ae965f1b935a812811742330b4dfc.png)

Now, let $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ be a point that lies on $\mathbf r(t)$ for some $t = t_0$ that is an extrema (max or min) of $f.$

Since $g(x,y,z)=a$ and $h(x,y,z)=b$ are level surfaces of the functions $g(x,y,z)$ and $h(x,y,z),$ we have the following:

- $\nabla g$ is perpendicular to $g(x,y,z)=a$ at $P,$ and is therefore perpendicular to $\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$

- $\nabla h$ is perpendicular to $h(x,y,z)=b$ at $P,$ and is therefore perpendicular to $\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$

The situation is sketched below.

![](images/16/16f2f1818628d9eb12ed0f3f2834cd916101839362813afe1be3f90ea35dd104.png)

Let's now compute $\big[f(\mathbf r(t))\big]',$ the derivative of $f$ over the curve $\mathbf r(t).$ By the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[f(r(t))]^{′} & =[f(x(t),y(t),z(t))]^{′} \\  & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\cdot {x}^{′}(t)+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\cdot {y}^{′}(t)+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\cdot {z}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩\cdot ⟨{x}^{′}(t),{y}^{′}(t),{z}^{′}(t)⟩ \\  & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $P$ is an extremum, we must have 

$$
\big[f(\mathbf{r}(t_0))\big]' = 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t_0)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t_0) = 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t_0)) \perp \mathbf{r}'(t_0).
$$

Since $\mathbf{r}'(t_0)$ is tangent to $\mathbf r(t)$ at $P,$ we have that $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t_0))$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf r(t)$ at $P.$

So, $\nabla g$ and $\nabla h$ are both perpendicular to $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $P$. Assuming they aren't parallel, they span the two-dimensional space perpendicular to $\mathbf{r}(t)$. Now $\nabla f$ is also perpendicular to $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $P$. This means that $\nabla f$ lies in the plane spanned by $\nabla g$ and $\nabla h.$ This condition can be represented by the following equation:

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y,z) + \mu \nabla h(x,y,z),
$$

where the real numbers $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are the Lagrange multipliers.

"Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\pm 3\text{i}.$*

| ${e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}\,\,$ |  | $3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ | $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3\text{i}t) & ={e}^{3\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot 3\text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+3{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5{\alpha }_{1}t & =-5\cdot \frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308658 :question/id #uuid "b1c86e08-63ee-5a97-b95f-27068e31ae61" :question/math-academy-id "q-334635"} {:db/id 17592186308659 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186308300}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $3,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $3t$ | $1-3t$ |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(3t) &={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =6{e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1+3t), \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3{e}^{3t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1+3t & -3t \\ 3t & 1-3t\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308671 :question/id #uuid "3361c13c-b482-5551-8d22-7ff3a0ff8596" :question/math-academy-id "q-334732"} {:db/id 17592186308672 :question/id #uuid "4bf1a0f0-bb87-5dac-ad3b-1ce93c87e2a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-334733" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186221410 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0fd1d280-c768-5504-892e-a9a1948e1f1a" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52b1d7ae-e4dd-5799-9115-e6e7b1fd12ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12t" :db/id 17592186305951}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "52b1d7ae-e4dd-5799-9115-e6e7b1fd12ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12t" :db/id 17592186305951} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dde19ef-9af0-5255-a3d4-655b000140c4" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186307818} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fc7ea02-06bd-5e6c-aed2-4751d80186b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1+6t" :db/id 17592186305289}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "0fc7ea02-06bd-5e6c-aed2-4751d80186b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1+6t" :db/id 17592186305289} :answer-field/id #uuid "893c4189-3f31-573e-94ae-26b874312a53" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186307952}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -3 \\ 12 & -4\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $2,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | $-3t$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-2}} | $1-6t$ |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -3 \\ 12 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 12{\alpha }_{1}t & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =8{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1+6t) \\ 12{\alpha }_{1}t & =12{e}^{2t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1+6t & -3t \\ 12t & 1-6t\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308673 :question/id #uuid "05e36fef-5d87-510d-a2e4-12cce4dfd1e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-334734"} {:db/id 17592186308674 :question/id #uuid 17592186050054 :topic/id #uuid "29ce72ae-dbea-5d83-a81d-90545461cdec" :topic/math-academy-id 6375} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222306 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222473 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to compute the **matrix exponential**.

Recall that the scalar exponential function $e^t$ can be written as the power series 

$$
e^t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{t^k}{k!} = 1 + t + \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!} + \cdots.
$$

Now, let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix. By definition, the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ is given by the analogous series

$$
e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!} = I + tA + \dfrac{t^2}{2}A^2 + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!}A^k + \cdots.
$$

There are several approaches for computing matrix exponentials:

- The most direct approach is to use the definition above, but this is typically impractical.

- Another method, often covered in linear algebra courses, is to use the Jordan canonical form of $A$. This works, but it can also be tedious, especially for larger matrices.

Here, we will introduce a different method.

By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, every power $A^n, A^{n+1}, \ldots$ can be rewritten as a linear combination of 

$$
I, \: A, \: A^2, \: \ldots, \: A^{n-1}.
$$

As a result, $e^{At}$ can be written in the form

$$
e^{At}=\alpha_{n-1}A^{n-1} t^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2} A^{n-2}t^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1 At+\alpha_0 I,
$$

where $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n-1}$ are functions of $t$ and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. 

Now, we define the polynomial 

$$
r(\lambda)=\alpha_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.
$$

Then we have the following key fact:

> For any eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $At$, we have $r(\lambda) = e^{\lambda}.$

Let’s now see how this method works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "d78b3664-4117-56fc-bf30-5ca3acb28377" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f932ab79-9fa6-5a87-aa94-755b1685c4e3" :step/math-academy-id 588472 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222307}} {:db/id 17592186222307 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222482 :tutorial/content "Let's find $e^{At}$ for $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}$ 

By solving the characteristic polynomial $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we can find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2, \qquad
\lambda_2=7.
$$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2t, \qquad
\lambda_2=7t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,\Rightarrow \,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
5t\alpha_1 = e^{7t} - e^{2t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_1 = \dfrac{1}{5t}\bigl(e^{7t}-e^{2t}\bigr).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $7$ and subtracting twice the second one, we get

$$
5\alpha_0 = 7e^{2t} - 2e^{7t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((2{e}^{7t}-2{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & =-7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{7}{5}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((7{e}^{7t}-7{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 7({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) & 5{e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e5aa695-b237-54d4-9836-20514d70dc9e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14389 :tutorial/title "2x2 Matrices With Distinct Real Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "3c91134a-154b-5692-a2cc-fdc45c81af7e" :step/math-academy-id 588473 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222308}} {:db/id 17592186222308 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221408 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221150 :question/id #uuid "35a158c3-37b6-5123-ba90-1fd05218ce43" :question/math-academy-id "e-21271"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fee186e0-579f-5104-b0e1-50540abc0bdc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050001}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221925} {:db/id 17592186221994} {:db/id 17592186308532} {:db/id 17592186308533} {:db/id 17592186308644} {:db/id 17592186308645}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Real Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "ebe4cfdc-9e1a-577d-ad38-9d117b4cf820" :step/math-academy-id 588474 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222309}} {:db/id 17592186222309 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221409 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221151 :question/id #uuid "18064c11-63d3-599a-b504-7b589f46c3dc" :question/math-academy-id "e-21272"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a118fe4a-cd1f-52f7-aa33-59f5494e4905" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048305}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221932} {:db/id 17592186222002} {:db/id 17592186308654} {:db/id 17592186308655} {:db/id 17592186308656} {:db/id 17592186308657} {:db/id 17592186308658} {:db/id 17592186308659} {:db/id 17592186308660} {:db/id 17592186370129}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "ea0b2d60-3227-5e25-b6a9-171c0dc66319" :step/math-academy-id 588478 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222310}} {:db/id 17592186222310 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222481 :tutorial/content "Recall that the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ can be written as

>

Let's apply these facts to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "d7b15b25-b73f-5d5f-aa02-e4c1a5e9804e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14388 :tutorial/title "2x2 Matrices With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "855a741b-2bbe-5e04-b892-8d1d9c7d0e65" :step/math-academy-id 588481 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222311}} {:db/id 17592186222311 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221410 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221152 :question/id #uuid "40a6318a-a1c9-55f3-afdb-02b43891d7b5" :question/math-academy-id "e-21273"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0fd1d280-c768-5504-892e-a9a1948e1f1a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221933} {:db/id 17592186222003} {:db/id 17592186308670} {:db/id 17592186308671} {:db/id 17592186308672} {:db/id 17592186308673} {:db/id 17592186308674} {:db/id 17592186308675} {:db/id 17592186370138}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "de5a7d5c-0c01-5247-8ba6-a69a863c9cbb" :step/math-academy-id 588482 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222312}} {:db/id 17592186222312 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222505 :tutorial/content "Again, let $A$ be a constant $n\times n$ matrix. The matrix exponential satisfies

$$
\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\bigl(e^{At}\bigr)=A\,e^{At}.
$$

Indeed, recall that

$$
e^{At}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(At)^k}{k!}
=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!}.
$$

To prove the formula, we differentiate the series above term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}) & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k}\cdot k{t}^{k-1}}{k!} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k}{t}^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \\  & =A{\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k-1}{t}^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \\  & =A{\sum }_{j=0}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{j}{t}^{j}}{j!} \\  & =A\,{e}^{At}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "739548ab-310c-5de3-a426-1fcaa3282478" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14526 :tutorial/title "Derivatives of Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "fc10fbf4-2be0-5b3f-ad2e-0505b175d5a6" :step/math-academy-id 588485 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222313}} {:db/id 17592186222313 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221411 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221194 :question/id #uuid "c0213c76-94e8-5ab3-a260-8a78a205589a" :question/math-academy-id "e-21724"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d4fc3ba4-d488-5156-88dc-837369269cef" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221995} {:db/id 17592186222006} {:db/id 17592186308726} {:db/id 17592186308727} {:db/id 17592186308728} {:db/id 17592186308729} {:db/id 17592186308730} {:db/id 17592186308731} {:db/id 17592186308732} {:db/id 17592186370312} {:db/id 17592186370321}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Derivative of a Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "df4956ab-0323-513e-ab21-66734987f4d0" :step/math-academy-id 588486 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222314}} {:db/id 17592186222314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222506 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials have other properties. We list a few of them:

- *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

$$
e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
$$

- *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

$$
(e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
$$

- *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

$$
e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
$$

- *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

$$
e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
$$

**Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute." :tutorial/id #uuid "2fcc3801-5d58-5c8e-b8c8-7be65b34f71a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14527 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "24b8ab46-a4b1-5358-abbd-db086f102dbf" :step/math-academy-id 588489}] :activity/title "Matrix Exponentials" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221467} {:db/id 17592186222306 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222473 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to compute the **matrix exponential**.

Recall that the scalar exponential function $e^t$ can be written as the power series 

$$
e^t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{t^k}{k!} = 1 + t + \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!} + \cdots.
$$

Now, let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix. By definition, the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ is given by the analogous series

$$
e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!} = I + tA + \dfrac{t^2}{2}A^2 + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!}A^k + \cdots.
$$

There are several approaches for computing matrix exponentials:

- The most direct approach is to use the definition above, but this is typically impractical.

- Another method, often covered in linear algebra courses, is to use the Jordan canonical form of $A$. This works, but it can also be tedious, especially for larger matrices.

Here, we will introduce a different method.

By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, every power $A^n, A^{n+1}, \ldots$ can be rewritten as a linear combination of 

$$
I, \: A, \: A^2, \: \ldots, \: A^{n-1}.
$$

As a result, $e^{At}$ can be written in the form

$$
e^{At}=\alpha_{n-1}A^{n-1} t^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2} A^{n-2}t^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1 At+\alpha_0 I,
$$

where $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n-1}$ are functions of $t$ and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. 

Now, we define the polynomial 

$$
r(\lambda)=\alpha_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.
$$

Then we have the following key fact:

> For any eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $At$, we have $r(\lambda) = e^{\lambda}.$

Let’s now see how this method works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "d78b3664-4117-56fc-bf30-5ca3acb28377" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f932ab79-9fa6-5a87-aa94-755b1685c4e3" :step/math-academy-id 588472 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222307}} {:db/id 17592186222473 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to compute the **matrix exponential**.

Recall that the scalar exponential function $e^t$ can be written as the power series 

$$
e^t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{t^k}{k!} = 1 + t + \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!} + \cdots.
$$

Now, let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix. By definition, the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ is given by the analogous series

$$
e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!} = I + tA + \dfrac{t^2}{2}A^2 + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!}A^k + \cdots.
$$

There are several approaches for computing matrix exponentials:

- The most direct approach is to use the definition above, but this is typically impractical.

- Another method, often covered in linear algebra courses, is to use the Jordan canonical form of $A$. This works, but it can also be tedious, especially for larger matrices.

Here, we will introduce a different method.

By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, every power $A^n, A^{n+1}, \ldots$ can be rewritten as a linear combination of 

$$
I, \: A, \: A^2, \: \ldots, \: A^{n-1}.
$$

As a result, $e^{At}$ can be written in the form

$$
e^{At}=\alpha_{n-1}A^{n-1} t^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2} A^{n-2}t^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1 At+\alpha_0 I,
$$

where $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n-1}$ are functions of $t$ and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. 

Now, we define the polynomial 

$$
r(\lambda)=\alpha_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.
$$

Then we have the following key fact:

> For any eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $At$, we have $r(\lambda) = e^{\lambda}.$

Let’s now see how this method works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "d78b3664-4117-56fc-bf30-5ca3acb28377" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186222307 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222482 :tutorial/content "Let's find $e^{At}$ for $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}$ 

By solving the characteristic polynomial $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we can find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2, \qquad
\lambda_2=7.
$$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2t, \qquad
\lambda_2=7t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,\Rightarrow \,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
5t\alpha_1 = e^{7t} - e^{2t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_1 = \dfrac{1}{5t}\bigl(e^{7t}-e^{2t}\bigr).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $7$ and subtracting twice the second one, we get

$$
5\alpha_0 = 7e^{2t} - 2e^{7t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{5}\bigl(7e^{2t}-2e^{7t}\bigr).
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((2{e}^{7t}-2{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & =-7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{7}{5}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((7{e}^{7t}-7{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 7({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) & 5{e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e5aa695-b237-54d4-9836-20514d70dc9e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14389 :tutorial/title "2x2 Matrices With Distinct Real Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "3c91134a-154b-5692-a2cc-fdc45c81af7e" :step/math-academy-id 588473 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222308}} {:db/id 17592186222482 :tutorial/content "Let's find $e^{At}$ for $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}$

The matrix exponential satisfies

$$
\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\bigl(e^{At}\bigr)=A\,e^{At}.

Indeed, recall that

$$
e^{At}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(At)^k}{k!}
=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!}.
$$

To prove the formula, we differentiate the series above term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}) & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k}\cdot k{t}^{k-1}}{k!} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k}{t}^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \\  & =A{\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k-1}{t}^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \\  & =A{\sum }_{j=0}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{j}{t}^{j}}{j!} \\  & =A\,{e}^{At}\end{aligned}

We list a few of them:

- *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

$$
e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
$$

- *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

$$
(e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
$$

- *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

$$
e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
$$

- *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

$$
e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
$$

**Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute." :tutorial/id #uuid "2fcc3801-5d58-5c8e-b8c8-7be65b34f71a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14527 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "24b8ab46-a4b1-5358-abbd-db086f102dbf" :step/math-academy-id 588489} {:db/id 17592186222506 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials have other properties. ![](images/a6/a60ddaebcf32cd8d69624b79f34d96d8ca1c18ec59c8bc443a95e235dedfae9e.png)" :question/worked-solution "In the picture, we are given a half-cone with the $z$-axis as its axis.

We write the position of a point (vector) in spherical polar coordinates as $(\rho,\theta,\phi),$ where 

- $\rho \geq 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

- ${\color{black}\theta}\in [0, 2\pi)$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

- $\phi \in [0, \pi]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

Every point on the given half-cone makes an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ radians with the positive $z$-axis. On the other hand, $\rho$ and $\theta$ can vary arbitrarily in their respective domains. 

Therefore, the spherical polar equation of the surface is $\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$"} {:db/id 17592186176184 :question/id #uuid "52ca5532-94f1-527a-af84-d4e9f2c326d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-102943" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186175966 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "133f6b90-4074-5860-9b89-16b59c5613bf" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Spherical Representation of a Surface From an Image"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "89f34521-0fe5-5dba-b5ce-bfd1f7994983" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "r = \frac{π}{3}ϕ" :db/id 17592186173363} {:answer/id #uuid "0c45931a-20a8-5647-b35c-95e54c97ada0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "θ = \frac{π}{3}" :db/id 17592186173364} {:answer/id #uuid "334d3c0a-e4ec-5bc6-8d30-b38115263b7b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "ϕ = \frac{π}{3}" :db/id 17592186173365} {:answer/id #uuid "5080f036-e062-5cfe-b10c-f6140a353ec5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "r = \frac{π}{3}θ" :db/id 17592186173366} {:answer/id #uuid "738b93f6-729c-5dec-af6c-792776649438" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "r = \frac{π}{4}" :db/id 17592186173367}] :answer-field/id #uuid "e03fafa7-5de5-5b87-8159-28addb0e0b3c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186173362}] :question/problem "![](images/ae/ae59540093c131582cf3d7c682a093eea6cbced9d8c88975a925e5c1d71123f9.png)

- $\rho \geq 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

- ${\color{black}\theta}\in [0, 2\pi)$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

- $\phi \in [0, \pi]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad
y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 
z = \rho\cos\phi
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents a half-sphere of radius $2$ centered at $(0,0,-2).$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x^2+y^2+z^2+4z=0$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4z & =0 \\ {\rho }^{2}+4\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & =0 \\ \rho (\rho +4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- $\rho \geq 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

- ${\color{black}\theta}\in [0, 2\pi)$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

- $\phi \in [0, \pi]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

When we fix one of these coordinates, we obtain some simple surfaces. Let's describe them:

- First, let's consider the equation

$$
\rho = c,
$$

for $c \gt 0.$ This equation describes the set of points on a surface whose distance from the origin equals $c.$ So, we obtain a sphere of radius $c$ centered at $O.$ 

![](images/1a/1aaecd51b8699f9a537496fa3bd581e153360eec3ef0e4bff4748c9ba3254a55.png)

- Next, consider the equation 

$$
\theta=c,
$$

 
where $c\in [0,2\pi).$ This equation describes the set of points that make an angle of $c$ radians with the positive $x$-axis. Therefore, we obtain a *half-plane* whose boundary is the $z$-axis.

![](images/5a/5a4e9d6481978b148ae696b73e75859808095856aacb269a2069dd3265be8684.png)

- Finally, consider the equation

$$
\phi = c,
$$

where $c\in (0,\pi).$ This equation describes the set of points that make an angle of $c$ radians with the positive $z$-axis. Therefore, we obtain a *half-cone* whose axis is the $z$-axis.

What is the value of $y_1 + y_2$?" :question/worked-solution "We need to solve the following system consisting of the equations of the curves:

$$
{y =-x^{2} + x + 4; y = 2x + 2
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
-x^{2} + x + 4 &= 2x + 2 \\
- x^{2} - x + 2 &= 0 \\
- (x^{2} + x - 2) &= 0 \\
- (x + 2)(x - 1) &= 0 \\
x &= -2, 1
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are $x_1 = -2$ and $x_2 = 1$.

To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either the curve or the line. Let's choose the line since it's simpler.

- Substituting $x=-2$, we get
$y|= 2x + 2; = 2(-2) + 2; =-2$,
so one point of intersection is $(-2,-2)$.
- Substituting $x=1$, we get
$y|= 2x + 2; = 2(1) + 2; = 4$,
so the other point of intersection is $(1,4)$.

The points of intersection are $(-2,-2)$ and $(1,4)$. Therefore,

$$
y_1 = -2,\; y_2 = 4
$$

and

$$
y_1 + y_2 = -2 + 4 = 2
$$

$$
{y =-x^{2} + 6x; y = 9
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
-x^{2} + 6x &= 9 \\
- x^{2} + 6x - 9 &= 0 \\
- (x^{2} - 6x + 9) &= 0 \\
- (x - 3)(x - 3) &= 0 \\
x &= 3
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $x$-coordinate of the intersection point is $x=3$.

We know the $y$-coordinate of the intersection point from the equation of the line. So, the only point of intersection is $(3, 9)$. Therefore, $p=3,\; q=9$, and

$$
p+q = 3+9 = 12
$$

$$
y=x +2k
$$

intersects the parabola

$$
y=x^2-x+3
$$

we need to solve the following system of equations for the two curves:

$$
{y = x^{2} - x + 3; y = x + 2k
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and writing in standard form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - x + 3 &= x + 2k \\
x^{2} - 2x + 3 - 2k &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve this equation using the quadratic formula with

$$
a=1,\, b=-2
$$

and $c=3-2k{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= (- (-2) ± \sqrt{(-2)^{2} - 4(1)(3 - 2k)})/(2(1)) \\
&= \frac{2 ± \sqrt{4 - 12 + 8k}}{2} \\
&= \frac{2 ± \sqrt{8k - 8}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the line and parabola do not intersect, our quadratic equation must have no real solutions; hence, the expression inside the square root must be negative.
Setting up and solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}8k - 8 & < 0 \\ 8k & < 8 \\ k & < 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the range of possible values of $k$ is $k \lt 1$."} {:db/id 17592186050334 :topic/id #uuid "40c0038d-ae3b-525b-803b-462840adecbb" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186068832 :tutorial/content "Consider the line

$$
y = x + 2
$$

and the parabola

$$
y = x^2 + x + 1
$$

shown in the graph below.

![](images/9d/9d7ca10163c9b5096f90e19bdb50d98881bd55e92cbaea4aa5af6696e728f9f3.png)

We can see from the diagram that there are two points of intersection. So let's calculate the coordinates of these intersection points.

An intersection point is a common solution of the equations

$$
y = x + 2
$$

and

$$
y = x^2 + x + 1
$$

In other words, to get the coordinates of the intersection points, we have to solve the following system of equations:

$$
{y = x^{2} + x + 1; y = x + 2
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and then solving for $x$ using our knowledge of quadratic equations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} + x + 1 &= x + 2 \\
x^{2} + x + 1 &= x + 2 \\
x^{2} + 1 &= 2 \\
x^{2} - 1 &= 0 \\
(x + 1)(x - 1) &= 0 \\
x &= -1, 1
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are $x=-1$ and $x=1$.

To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either curve. Let's choose the line since it's simpler.

- Substituting $x=-1$, we get
$y|= x + 2; = (-1) + 2; = 1$,
so one point of intersection is $(-1,1)$.
- Substituting $x=1$, we get
$y|= x + 2; = (1) + 2; = 3$,
so the other point of intersection is $(1,3)$.

Therefore, we conclude that the points of intersection are

$$
\left(-1,\,1 \right)
$$

and

$$
\left(1,\,3 \right)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b907a9fb-d730-5d33-b47d-e448e4bc64dd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13862 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a89077dd-e912-5270-b496-6fe6281d817b" :step/math-academy-id 509403 :step/next {:db/id 17592186217981}} {:db/id 17592186217981 :step/content {:db/id 17592186217108 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186216959 :question/id #uuid "44ed3aff-8a4b-520c-808f-9e3ff928ac74" :question/math-academy-id "e-19814"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "31b2bec9-3dff-557c-8cf5-a54f145fc45c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049869} {:db/id 17592186049919} {:db/id 17592186050984}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186217329} {:db/id 17592186217334}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the X-Coordinates of the Intersection Points of a Parabola and a Line"} :step/id #uuid "1e5979d0-7029-563e-b231-e335fadaa16d" :step/math-academy-id 509404 :step/next {:db/id 17592186217982}} {:db/id 17592186217982 :step/content {:db/id 17592186217109 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186216960 :question/id #uuid "9aa14c81-aeaa-51b7-9d16-468e22bc113d" :question/math-academy-id "e-19815"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "797cb8e2-0230-56ec-8fda-7f2b40a2329c" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186217330} {:db/id 17592186217335}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Y-Coordinates of the Intersection Points of a Parabola and a Line"} :step/id #uuid "67ccd293-c59d-59e8-a1d5-686a88bbfc0e" :step/math-academy-id 509408 :step/next {:db/id 17592186217983}} {:db/id 17592186217983 :step/content {:db/id 17592186218321 :tutorial/content "![](images/b9/b9cb25bbb7b3076a3dae8688a232d18ec4092d68d9e815dedb438bc6900d97bb.png)

A line and a parabola may have **two**,
**one**, or **no** points of intersection.

This is similar to how a quadratic equation may have **two**,
**one**, or **no** solutions.

$$
y = x + 2
$$

and the parabola

$$
y = x^2 + x + 1
$$

shown in the graph below.

![](images/9d/9d7ca10163c9b5096f90e19bdb50d98881bd55e92cbaea4aa5af6696e728f9f3.png)

We can see from the diagram that there are two points of intersection. So let's calculate the coordinates of these intersection points.

An intersection point is a common solution of the equations

$$
y = x + 2
$$

and

$$
y = x^2 + x + 1
$$

In other words, to get the coordinates of the intersection points, we have to solve the following system of equations:

$$
{y = x^{2} + x + 1; y = x + 2
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and then solving for $x$ using our knowledge of quadratic equations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} + x + 1 &= x + 2 \\
x^{2} + x + 1 &= x + 2 \\
x^{2} + 1 &= 2 \\
x^{2} - 1 &= 0 \\
(x + 1)(x - 1) &= 0 \\
x &= -1, 1
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are $x=-1$ and $x=1$.

To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either curve. Let's choose the line since it's simpler.

- Substituting $x=-1$, we get
$y|= x + 2; = (-1) + 2; = 1$,
so one point of intersection is $(-1,1)$.
- Substituting $x=1$, we get
$y|= x + 2; = (1) + 2; = 3$,
so the other point of intersection is $(1,3)$.

Therefore, we conclude that the points of intersection are

$$
\left(-1,\,1 \right)
$$

and

$$
\left(1,\,3 \right)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b907a9fb-d730-5d33-b47d-e448e4bc64dd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13862 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a89077dd-e912-5270-b496-6fe6281d817b" :step/math-academy-id 509403 :step/next {:db/id 17592186217981}} {:db/id 17592186218320 :tutorial/content "Consider the line

:question/problem "Given the function
$f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = -7\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} + \left.3\|\mathbf{w}\\right|^2 - 2$
that maps two vectors to a scalar, find $\nabla_{\mathbf w} f$." :question/worked-solution "Using the results

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf w}(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}, \qquad \nabla_{\mathbf w} (\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{w}) = 2\mathbf{w}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
∇_{w}f &= ∇_{w}(-7w^{T}x + 3‖w‖^{2} - 2) \\
&=-7 \cdot ∇_{w}(w^{T}x) + 3 \cdot ∇_{w}(‖w‖^{2}) - ∇_{w}(2) \\
&=-7 \cdot ∇_{w}(w^{T}x) + 3 \cdot ∇_{w}(w^{T}w) - ∇_{w}(2) \\
&=-7 \cdot x + 3 \cdot 2w - 0 \\
&=-7x + 6w
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050758} {:db/id 17592186204569 :question/id #uuid "e4ea622d-252d-5ba8-893d-521c24e09b75" :question/math-academy-id "q-265043"} {:db/id 17592186204570 :question/id #uuid "a965b808-f42f-5f10-869c-9297170888dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-265044" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186204103 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b7de7a9a-4848-5590-b066-f746262181e5" :knowledge-point/title "Computing Gradients Including Squared Norms"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8333ad5c-643c-532a-a7ae-6d46ae048983" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "10w" :db/id 17592186203359} {:answer/id #uuid "96f16ea5-08aa-5ce8-982b-c204221184c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "10w + 4" :db/id 17592186203360} {:answer/id #uuid "bf677492-92fb-553b-bf5b-66a092456cb5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "10‖w‖" :db/id 17592186203361} {:answer/id #uuid "16b8fd77-ad53-5d58-817a-fb9b976ea1a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "20‖w‖" :db/id 17592186203362} {:answer/id #uuid "68af00de-549d-50da-a481-5462b4a43fcd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "20w" :db/id 17592186203363}] :answer-field/id #uuid "28d33f98-d0a8-57ab-93a4-44ca196a5226" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186203358}] :question/problem "Given the function

$f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \left.-3\left(\|\mathbf{w}\\right|_1\right)^3 - 5\mathbf x^T\mathbf w$
that maps a vector to a scalar, find $\nabla_{\mathbf w}f$. You may assume that $\mathbf w$ has no zero components." :question/worked-solution "Using the results

$$
\left.\nabla_{\mathbf w} (\|\mathbf{w}\\right|_1) = \text{sign}(\mathbf{w}), \qquad \nabla_{\mathbf w}\left(\mathbf x^T\mathbf w\right) = \mathbf x
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
∇_{w}f &= ∇_{w}(-3(‖w‖_{1})^{3} - 5x^{T}w) \\
&= ∇_{w}(-3(‖w‖_{1})^{3}) - ∇_{w}(5x^{T}w) \\
&=-3 \cdot ∇_{w}((‖w‖_{1})^{3}) - 5 \cdot ∇_{w}(x^{T}w) \\
&=-3 \cdot 3(‖w‖_{1})^{2} \cdot ∇_{w}(‖w‖_{1}) - 5 \cdot x \\
&=-3 \cdot 3(‖w‖_{1})^{2} \cdot sign(w) - 5 \cdot x \\
&=-9(‖w‖_{1})^{2} \cdot sign(w) - 5x
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048367} {:db/id 17592186204568 :question/id #uuid "f4e7ed0e-c09d-52a0-9771-61764066a618" :question/math-academy-id "q-265042"} {:db/id 17592186204592 :question/id #uuid "662b9c53-b55a-5b63-9768-b5b6d98e927b" :question/math-academy-id "q-275961" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186204104 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "86b3efb7-511d-5da7-92ca-5add976b1ca1" :knowledge-point/title "Computing Gradients of Functions Containing L1 Norms"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b79cb89c-573b-5910-8228-e4a951e60162" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12sign(w) + w" :db/id 17592186203468} {:answer/id #uuid "f5c2815b-251d-5dce-a377-f450d1c146df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12(‖w‖_{1})^{2} \cdot sign(w) + w" :db/id 17592186203469} {:answer/id #uuid "4657f2b0-5054-55b3-927e-bb8766777bd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12sign(w) + 2x" :db/id 17592186203470} {:answer/id #uuid "7218b082-798f-56ba-8aa9-14ccfce9d5b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12(‖w‖_{1})^{2} \cdot sign(w) + x" :db/id 17592186203471} {:answer/id #uuid "7fc98d41-0f58-530e-b9ec-19927f41c472" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6sign(w) + x" :db/id 17592186203472}] :answer-field/id #uuid "2e221444-1ca4-5f83-b8a3-c4d4f75a3ed7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186203467}] :question/problem "Given the function
