$$
\begin{aligned}3y{x}^{2} & =48+3x{y}^{2} \\ 3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2} & =48\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=48.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2})j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}-6xy)i-(6xy-3{y}^{2})j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot (i-j)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot (i-j) & =0 \\ ((3{x}^{2}-6xy)i-(6xy-3{y}^{2})j)\cdot (i-j) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-6xy+6xy-3{y}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-y)(x+y) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=y$ or $x=-y.$ Substituting $x=y$ into the equation of our curve gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y{x}^{2} & =48+3x{y}^{2} \\ 3y{y}^{2} & =48+3y{y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{3} & =48+3{y}^{3} \\ 0 & =48\end{aligned}
$$

Since we get a false statement, we conclude that does not exist points of the form $(x,x)$ on the curve. Substituting $x=-y$ into the equation of our curve gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y{x}^{2} & =48+3x{y}^{2} \\ 3y(-y)^{2} & =48+3(-y){y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{3} & =48-3{y}^{3} \\ 6{y}^{3} & =48 \\ {y}^{3} & =8 \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{8} \\ y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $y=2$, we get $x=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,2).$"} {:db/id 17592186521756 :question/id #uuid "0e539d3d-4951-53af-94a7-c8aeb37adea8"} {:db/id 17592186521758 :question/id #uuid "10aa9a22-24d9-5578-9f7c-cc0b57f6bc72"} {:db/id 17592186521761 :question/id #uuid "138b2fa1-5696-5cfb-b4c1-4b8eecec9f34"} {:db/id 17592186521800 :question/id #uuid "5284e034-941a-5de0-a7ad-3718d5b22f4c"} {:db/id 17592186521807 :question/id #uuid "638eb9ae-09f8-5fce-b7bc-2aac37c3181f"} {:db/id 17592186521812 :question/id #uuid "714feb07-8211-5226-a523-87577689d617"} {:db/id 17592186521815 :question/id #uuid "76dd91ba-d91e-5c6c-a612-22de10fca4c2"} {:db/id 17592186521832 :question/id #uuid "a3e58fdb-d0b9-56b1-bc61-4cc0137e18be"} {:db/id 17592186521863 :question/id #uuid "e7a17a4a-d80f-51f1-afa6-1faeaa5943f8"} {:db/id 17592186521870 :question/id #uuid "f0a0a0dc-dc0e-505f-ae57-9fc7b81e15fb"} {:db/id 17592186048554} {:db/id 17592186049617} {:db/id 17592186049696 :topic/difficulty 0.8681639855309368 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428494 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. 17592186045486} :question/problem "Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}=(x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3},\,\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}=6x{z}^{2}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}
$$" :question/worked-solution "As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3}) \\  & =(x{y}^{2}+2y)\cdot x{e}^{xy}+(2xy+2)\cdot {e}^{xy}+0 \\  & =({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4xy+2){e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(6x{z}^{2}) \\  & =12xz.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =(0+0+2){e}^{0}=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =12(1)(1)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =2+12=14.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268928 :question/id #uuid "f5acd057-670a-5a23-995b-650a92790dc3" :question/math-academy-id "q-133371"} {:db/id 17592186268929 :question/id #uuid "33686134-3f7d-5a05-9109-0d2ac79b776f" :question/math-academy-id "q-133373" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5f60ae37-1165-5440-bde6-f01cffce801b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186266987} {:answer/id #uuid "8e8382b2-cf1c-5bb5-b534-beacbde2bdfb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186267414} {:answer/id #uuid "a7b8eef4-ff75-5267-860e-a762c49305b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186267662} {:answer/id #uuid "c4658edd-5348-55cc-a2aa-5ce494911f0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186267898} {:answer/id #uuid "f3239213-7c2d-5989-a3bf-a19a7229c158" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186268307}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186267414} :answer-field/id #uuid "a30a187b-9301-5273-a095-e7add20e9085" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268696}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate ${f}_{yxy}(6,\frac{\pi }{3})$ if ${f}_{xy}(x,y)=7+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$" :question/worked-solution "As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxy}(x,y) & ={f}_{xyy}(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{xy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(7+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(6,\frac{\pi }{3}):$

$$
{f}_{yxy}(6,\frac{\pi }{3})=6\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})=3
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268930 :question/id #uuid "9379a450-3ef7-54fa-b6cb-c35ea0f78eee" :question/math-academy-id "q-133382" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b6c9d7c-6f8b-549f-ade8-d1e4ebbf0134" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186266377} {:answer/id #uuid "2db15dbd-e51f-532f-9bfd-157b9f779945" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186266548} {:answer/id #uuid "3c660db5-3c31-5643-8113-78583f356468" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186266674} {:answer/id #uuid "a5eecdbb-ca77-56e2-9dcd-5a6810654073" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186267646} {:answer/id #uuid "f8a5f3a4-eed9-50d5-8e07-a411ebbe09d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186268346}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186266377} :answer-field/id #uuid "50bb18b4-57b1-5ebe-9423-935bc3b0a3cc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268551}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}=\frac{x{e}^{yz}}{x+y},\,\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}=-\frac{z{e}^{yz}}{x+y}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,1,0):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂x∂y}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}
$$" :question/worked-solution "As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x{e}^{yz}}{x+y}) \\  & ={e}^{yz}\cdot (\frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{yz}}{(x+y)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-\frac{z{e}^{yz}}{x+y}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}\cdot ({e}^{yz}+yz{e}^{yz}) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{yz}(1+yz)}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =\frac{1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}}{(1+1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =-\frac{{e}^{1\cdot 0}(1+1\cdot 0)}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,1,0)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268931 :question/id #uuid "4cca6146-d9c7-5b1f-ad16-9d00e8365a81" :question/math-academy-id "q-133395"} {:db/id 17592186323822 :question/id #uuid :question/problem "Consider that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first, second and third-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ What is the value of ${f}_{yxy}(1,0)-{f}_{yy}(1,0)-{f}_{xyy}(1,0)$ given that ${f}_{yy}(x,y)={x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡xy?$" :question/worked-solution "As the function and its first, second, and third-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ we must have ${f}_{yxy}(x,y)={f}_{xyy}(x,y).$ 

Therefore, we can swap the order of the subscripts in the first term. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxy}(1,0)-{f}_{yy}(1,0)-{f}_{xyy}(1,0) & ={f}_{xyy}(1,0)-{f}_{yy}(1,0)-{f}_{xyy}(1,0) \\  & =\cancel{{f}_{xyy}(1,0)}-{f}_{yy}(1,0)-\cancel{{f}_{xyy}(1,0)} \\  & =-{f}_{yy}(1,0) \\  & =-(1)^{3}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 0) \\  & =-1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186409651 :question/id #uuid "923e8280-3481-5e90-8081-225a78ef2cea" :question/math-academy-id "q-133393" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4421a8c6-aea6-5d62-9cd0-8a06f8915dcd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186409638} {:answer/id #uuid "45730328-f0dc-5c33-a6c2-53d71d04445d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186409639} {:answer/id #uuid "4d58c242-f6fd-5d67-8e96-0273fcae35a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186409641} {:answer/id #uuid "59fd5070-c975-5965-b9d4-d62ba5834853" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186409642} {:answer/id #uuid "d26ca855-4a28-50fd-bba1-040fec87c89e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186409647}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186409642} :answer-field/id #uuid "504a276b-9fed-5959-a86c-c2b987992901" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409648}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Evaluate ${f}_{zxz}(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ given that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{zz}(x,y,z)=2z\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y)+x{e}^{z-2y}
$$" :question/worked-solution "As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zzx}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{zxz}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zz}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2z\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y)+x{e}^{z-2y}) \\  & =2z\cdot \frac{1}{x-2y}+{e}^{z-2y} \\  & =\frac{2z}{x-2y}+{e}^{z-2y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point  $(2,\frac{1}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zxz}(2,\frac{1}{2},1) & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}}+{e}^{1-2\cdot 1/2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2-1}+{e}^{1-1} \\  & =2+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186437088 :question/id #uuid "17f2fd35-823f-52a1-8bc6-17fa0dd0fd8c" :question/math-academy-id "q-133394"} {:db/id 17592186479870 :question/id #uuid "87b5b3e0-dcda-563d-b53d-0df7f66aab12" :question/math-academy-id "q-65129" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23f5ce90-f71e-52dc-8beb-408f7faeaa27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186479415} {:answer/id #uuid "48a543dd-5073-5eff-a396-7a9535994086" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186479465} {:answer/id #uuid "4a8aa56b-9b6e-5e43-81d5-2db6976aeebe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2+\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186479471} {:answer/id #uuid "684701da-26b3-560c-8537-f88180932fce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2+\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186479514} {:answer/id #uuid "eeb1a895-8ba1-56dc-9e30-7108e7d80a9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186479711}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186479415} :answer-field/id #uuid "50f2ed47-78e7-59d4-a40f-57fb0a2f9402" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186479770}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate ${f}_{yxy}(1,\frac{\pi }{2})$ if ${f}_{yy}(x,y)=-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).$" :question/worked-solution "As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. - **III.** ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={e}^{y}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+4y)=4 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x-y)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(0)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =0+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y, \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =0-\operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'."} {:db/id 17592186125186 :question/id #uuid "3caf1655-4ce4-5a5f-995b-a06e33069b3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-65127" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e6926f5e-dc21-5da5-b35d-b718df8a66ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186477365} {:answer/id #uuid "f0f6a95f-1511-52d2-946b-1d648665d214" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186477366}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186477365} :answer-field/id #uuid "c6da62ee-a826-5879-91f1-9c7966d71193" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186477652} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f4cb90f6-70fc-53f0-9088-772c160341cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186477367} {:answer/id #uuid "26573f3b-930d-57c0-9106-c38022948389" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186477368}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186477368} :answer-field/id #uuid "23b11426-2cab-5199-bc57-42df399c747e" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186477653} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9478de04-8fb1-57f2-973d-3770f1978c1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186477369} {:answer/id #uuid "a7bf79dc-14ad-5ba5-85de-39e95f01562c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186477370}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186477370} :answer-field/id #uuid "766dd905-2ba1-5ac0-b3f1-1f815b83a4fe" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186477654}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+{y}^{2})=2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-y)=4y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+\sqrt{y})=1.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+{y}^{2})=2x+2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+2x)=2xy+2.\end{aligned}
$$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=x{e}^{xy}$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2y+1$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=2y+1$" :question/worked-solution "Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy}) \\  & ={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy} \\  & ={e}^{xy}(1+xy) \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{xy}) \\  & ={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy} \\  & ={e}^{xy}(1+xy).\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y+1)=2 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y+1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II only'."} {:db/id 17592186489263 :question/id #uuid "c68f1c1a-c6a6-5448-b77c-02d88ae0390d" :question/math-academy-id "q-36482" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5b45857f-4c74-59d9-8e35-85de5f5c9034" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186488645} {:answer/id #uuid "7d0ab324-a63f-56ba-b911-46caeedd3017" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186488721} {:answer/id #uuid "88ad4c18-6273-5c23-9f0f-fff73fe14cc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186488740} {:answer/id #uuid "a2acdb8d-7243-568f-a9db-fdae13525746" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186488792} {:answer/id #uuid "aed29a6c-7da5-5f41-b70d-1d66d427908e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186488818}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186488740} :answer-field/id #uuid "df0c4030-39f2-5bc9-a0e8-ac2b199792a8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186489148}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=y{x}^{2}-4y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-4x$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=3-5x$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=1$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-2{y}^{3}{e}^{{y}^{2}}$" :question/worked-solution "Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{x}^{2}-4y)={x}^{2}-4 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-4x)={x}^{2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3-5x)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =0+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-2{y}^{3}{e}^{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y-0 \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II only'."} {:db/id 17592186048859} {:db/id 17592186050869} {:db/id 17592186051085 :topic/difficulty 1.1334058414679022 :topic/id #uuid Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{curl}\,F=0$
- **II.** $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$
- **III.** $F$ is irrotational
- **IV.** $\text{curl}\,F$ points in the positive $z$-direction." :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

![](images/97/979b63f21e56924bd7880f9487cf829089e38cf14d287e70196c7a661e41f97f.png)

Moreover, if $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement I is true, whereas statement II is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would not rotate. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- Statement III is true. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ the vector field $F$ is irrotational.

- Statement IV is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ it points in neither the positive nor the negative $z$-direction.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186241116 :question/id #uuid "56135889-753b-5df4-829a-e16e02adbe8d" :question/math-academy-id "q-105692"} {:db/id 17592186241117 Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{curl}\,F=0$
- **II.** $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$
- **III.** $\text{curl}\,F$ points in the negative $z$-direction.
- **IV.** $F$ is irrotational" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

![](images/7c/7c831425eae7afd709d546a8e05100f495adc04bba6450cfa56d370b415a28f5.png)

If $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement II is true, whereas statement I is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would rotate clockwise. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- Statement III is true. Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (clockwise), our thumb will point into the screen. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F$ also points into from the screen, in the direction of decreasing $z.$

- Statement IV is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not irrotational.

:question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,j.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $F$ at the point $(\pi ,0).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(\pi ,0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(\pi ,0)} & =-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)-\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =0-\pi \cdot 1 \\  & =-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186235527 :question/id #uuid "a254e595-25b7-5631-ae7f-2ec647939f75" :question/math-academy-id "q-168118"} {:db/id 17592186262624 :question/id #uuid "84980841-460b-507f-8790-439efc8ff63f" :question/math-academy-id "q-126525" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "13264dd3-32ca-5425-ae4a-10ae592d25f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186260044} {:answer/id #uuid "1ad4275e-e84f-5e99-9926-6ed1c4bda7e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186260108} {:answer/id #uuid "5ec4d041-01f8-5cba-bbc5-711d818eb654" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186260692} {:answer/id #uuid "7344edf5-4fa2-53cc-aefd-2082b97c5134" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\pi }^{2}" :db/id 17592186260883} {:answer/id #uuid "deb142df-e54d-5f60-a501-f62bc2ccccc3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186261841}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260108} :answer-field/id #uuid "6208b069-a1cc-5b39-96a3-5295dfbd12c7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262291}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,i+(x{y}^{2}+1)\,j.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $F$ at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$

$$

:question/problem "Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+y=0,\,y(0)=4,\,{y}^{′}(0)=8.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=4$ into the general solution gives

$$
A=4.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=8,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=8$ into the above gives

$$
A+B=8.
$$

Using the fact that $A=4$ gives $B=4.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=4{e}^{x}+4x{e}^{x}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186152286 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151983 :question/id #uuid "88fe37cf-5df2-5988-90b8-082f7aaca609" :question/math-academy-id "e-6791"} :knowledge-point/id $$

$$
{y}^{″}+25y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A\operatorname{sin}⁡5x+B\operatorname{cos}⁡5x,
$$

solve the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{″}+25y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=5.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}B & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=5,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=5A\operatorname{cos}⁡5x-5B\operatorname{sin}⁡5x.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=5$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5=5A\,⟹\,A=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡5x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡5x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186152287 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186152008 :question/id #uuid "80968044-25e2-5906-929c-b944f84ca27d" :question/math-academy-id "e-7051"} :knowledge-point/id {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-2.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=2.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-{e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{e}^{-x}(-P\operatorname{sin}⁡x+Q\operatorname{cos}⁡x).
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=-2$ into the above to get

$$
-P+Q=-2.
$$

Using the fact that $P=2$ gives $Q=0.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348131 :question/id #uuid "9131a7ff-7e61-5a90-96bc-6b1cab75b7bc" :question/math-academy-id "q-7892"} {:db/id 17592186357627 :question/id #uuid "c3243450-c950-543f-968a-f0bf49df75ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-94025"} {:db/id 17592186357628 :question/id #uuid "ecd297d2-0d03-5232-81da-fdcaeb168238" :question/math-academy-id "q-94030" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4de3cea3-9ce1-5117-8440-1c848ea22d4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y={e}^{-3x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)" :db/id 17592186355356} {:answer/id #uuid "82b9aacb-816c-533f-8f18-7bad4adc1c9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y={e}^{-3x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)" :db/id 17592186355814} {:answer/id #uuid "90f20f88-ad66-5e68-9ff3-f7c959e067cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y={e}^{-3x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)" :db/id 17592186355943} {:answer/id #uuid "a0a0b4b1-1e9c-550c-b5cf-d7579feaa3f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y={e}^{-3x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)" :db/id 17592186356089} {:answer/id #uuid "f366d31e-4d24-5d08-beff-fd3ad156a6d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y={e}^{-3x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)" :db/id 17592186356793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356793} :answer-field/id #uuid "fdfe16cc-d998-5278-adcf-1b050e572699" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357355}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that the differential equation

{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),$ which is $5,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{2}{5}\cdot {5}^{2}=10\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186231570 :question/id #uuid "968f331f-040e-5a16-a459-23a91c08dfd4" :question/math-academy-id "q-343473" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "498bed50-28c7-50fa-a5df-0080495261c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186441791}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186441791} :answer-field/id #uuid "5abd7c36-14a4-56ef-ada9-6c206b80a9d0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186230295}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A particle of mass $0.5\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. {{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky+(3{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=3(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-1).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=3(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-1)$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$ Since

$$
f(t)=3(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-1)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $4.$

Therefore,

The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(6D-9Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-(6C+9Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 6D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-6C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-1$ and $D=-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Only solution III matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"."} {:db/id 17592186435718 :question/id #uuid "9d091e55-28a6-57e1-bec5-20aeba4179e3" :question/math-academy-id "q-343770"} {:db/id 17592186435720 :question/id #uuid "f5e9f5eb-87cf-56db-acd3-a7af3f0549dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-343755" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8098c12c-c69f-5410-91ea-5d34faacac72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186474792} {:answer/id #uuid "cbf8c1e6-7440-5b66-ac6a-a95e969d0c0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186474793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186474793} :answer-field/id #uuid "b0703231-e8db-5753-a623-8cdd5ed3035a" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186475322} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ebb008e-2a78-528f-b65f-04738d8d69bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186474794} {:answer/id #uuid "3b5fb8cd-1e60-5d1a-9b3c-43f1bdfb0eee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186474795}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186474794} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ee39774-5b22-57d7-b22d-32c67ba80ab1" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186475323} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "154527e1-d8e6-580a-bfa6-88b0d7e11c16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186474796} {:answer/id #uuid "fe8f9ab4-11d0-5d2b-b95a-f6633b354687" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186474797}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186474797} :answer-field/id #uuid "80d02f47-2169-5889-be5d-7762353c0de6" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186475324}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. :step/math-academy-id 612651 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231833}} {:db/id 17592186231833 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231987 :tutorial/content "Consider an undamped forced oscillator,

$$
y''+\omega^2y=f(t),
$$

where $\omega$ is the system's natural frequency. Its general solution is

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation $y''+\omega^2y=0$ and $y_p$ is any particular solution to the full equation.

Notice that the complementary solution can be written in any of the following equivalent forms:

1\. $y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi_1)}$

2\. $y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi_2)}$

3\. $y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}$

Now, suppose the external force has the resonant form

$$
f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),
$$

so that the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega.$

A sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega$ would duplicate $y_c,$ so at resonance we multiply by $t$ and use a trial of the form

$$
y_p=t\bigl(C\cos(\omega t)+D\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

To determine $C$ and $D,$ we first compute derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+t(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & =2(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t))-t{\omega }^{2}(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the equation, we have that the $t$-terms cancel out, and we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}{y}_{p}=2\omega D\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)-2\omega C\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we need $y_p''+\omega^2y_p=f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),$ equating coefficients gives

$$
2\omega D=a,
\qquad
-2\omega C=b.
$$

Therefore,

$$
C=-\frac{b}{2\omega},
\qquad
D=\frac{a}{2\omega},
$$

so a standard resonant particular solution is

$$
y_p =\frac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

So, when $f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t)$ and resonance occurs, the general solution can be written as

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y=A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)+\dfrac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr)}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b19a33b7-fd81-538c-8139-d44653c47533" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14777 :tutorial/title "General Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations With Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "35c65152-fe66-57ca-8c82-a01849b005d7" :step/math-academy-id 612654 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231834}} {:db/id 17592186231834 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231429 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231295 :question/id #uuid "f41473ff-05a6-5f3e-ae5b-0584810aa0dd" :question/math-academy-id "e-21878"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cac41120-247d-5821-b7f6-b342dbcf8f18" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231571} {:db/id 17592186231576} {:db/id 17592186317427} {:db/id 17592186317429} {:db/id 17592186317430} {:db/id 17592186317431} {:db/id 17592186317432} {:db/id 17592186317433} {:db/id 17592186427272} {:db/id 17592186435718} {:db/id 17592186435720} {:db/id 17592186442740}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations"} :step/id #uuid "eb6f14ff-8487-50a4-a45b-1ff02e60483d" :step/math-academy-id 612655 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231835}} {:db/id 17592186231835 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231988 :tutorial/content "Recall that resonance is the phenomenon where an external periodic force drives a vibrating system at exactly the system's natural frequency. In the undamped model, this causes the oscillations to grow larger and larger over time.

In the ideal undamped model, resonance produces a particular solution that grows in magnitude with time (due to the extra factor of $t$). This is why the model predicts that the amplitude increases *without bound*.

For example, consider the undamped forced oscillator

$$
y'' + 9y = \sin(3t).
$$

The complementary solution is of the form $y_c = A\cos(3t) + B\sin(3t),$ the natural frequency of the system is $\omega = 3,$ and the forcing frequency is also $3.$ Because these frequencies match, resonance occurs.

$$
y''+\omega^2y=f(t),
$$

where $\omega$ is the system's natural frequency. Its general solution is

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation $y''+\omega^2y=0$ and $y_p$ is any particular solution to the full equation.

Notice that the complementary solution can be written in any of the following equivalent forms:

1\. $y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi_1)}$

2\. $y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi_2)}$

3\. $y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}$

Now, suppose the external force has the resonant form

$$
f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),
$$

so that the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega.$

A sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega$ would duplicate $y_c,$ so at resonance we multiply by $t$ and use a trial of the form

$$
y_p=t\bigl(C\cos(\omega t)+D\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

To determine $C$ and $D,$ we first compute derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+t(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & =2(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t))-t{\omega }^{2}(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the equation, we have that the $t$-terms cancel out, and we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}{y}_{p}=2\omega D\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)-2\omega C\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we need $y_p''+\omega^2y_p=f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),$ equating coefficients gives

$$
2\omega D=a,
\qquad
-2\omega C=b.
$$

Therefore,

$$
C=-\frac{b}{2\omega},
\qquad
D=\frac{a}{2\omega},
$$

so a standard resonant particular solution is

$$
y_p =\frac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

So, when $f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t)$ and resonance occurs, the general solution can be written as

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y=A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)+\dfrac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr)}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b19a33b7-fd81-538c-8139-d44653c47533" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14777 :tutorial/title "General Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations With Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "35c65152-fe66-57ca-8c82-a01849b005d7" :step/math-academy-id 612654 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231834}} {:db/id 17592186231987 :tutorial/content "Consider an undamped forced oscillator,

{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),$ which is $5,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

The external force is $f(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).

$$

$$

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Only solution III matches the forms above.

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$

Equating coefficients, $C=0$ and $D=\frac{5}{8}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

$$

$$

{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),$ which is $4,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {4}^{2}=8\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4166c13b-ac53-51f9-9738-1fcaff73fb79" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481729}} {:db/id 17592186481691 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231571 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b10f3398-95fb-51ac-819d-349fa3583218" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186462315} {:answer/id #uuid "93d77f90-d255-502e-a3d2-a8904ab3576f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186462316}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186462316} :answer-field/id #uuid "d6a3385f-3cab-5129-83bb-f7a582ea68df" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462911} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15a268ac-7559-5f46-bf6c-3d1043ac53f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186462317} {:answer/id #uuid "47e07c54-ee13-5022-a287-d6f6ab82ff3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186462318}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186462317} :answer-field/id #uuid "2b82a872-8326-5513-8f4a-ccff55e33bb4" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462912} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aa10a572-2a12-5313-a511-b89c8f024781" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186462319} {:answer/id #uuid "f79ee182-a849-5b22-a888-28a5c0d2851d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186462320}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186462319} :answer-field/id #uuid "6dc60cb7-562c-5b04-bbc2-febf547f3bde" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186462913}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "28a570c8-4263-5a25-a7a9-87fb602a6de5" :question/math-academy-id "q-343490" :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)+3t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $1.$ Therefore,
$\omega =1.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =1$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(2D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡t-(2C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]+t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2D\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2C\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

Only solution I matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} :step/id #uuid "49ae1a21-0dd4-5aa8-8ab3-c3f8d983ec48" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481689}} {:db/id 17592186481702 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231576 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8588f05c-f259-5f6f-95a4-ba743efb8633" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None" :db/id 17592186230323} {:answer/id #uuid "87e2a5ac-5e6b-5176-ada3-76165f3827b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186230324} {:answer/id #uuid "bd0f684b-31be-53dd-959a-4c693200fbd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186230325} {:answer/id #uuid "ebbe1595-b0a0-5005-89d3-b1a66671386d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186230326} {:answer/id #uuid "6ad71e63-ab40-5319-b40d-20fec2c9d4de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186230327}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186230326} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6c1fc5b-ecb6-509b-ab8e-ba64d464ed59" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186230322}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a2dc0571-7d63-58c4-a7e9-b264e1dac3a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-343760" :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$

$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky-4sin\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=-8sin\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=-8sin\,(\frac{3}{2}t),$ which is $\frac{3}{2},$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

$$
k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}=\frac{9}{8}\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =4$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[16(D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-16(C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)]+16t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 16D\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-16C\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=0$ and $D=\frac{5}{8}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Only solution II matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"."} :step/id #uuid "65d89567-4925-56ab-9bcd-c0152afe9d34" :step/next {:db/id 17592186483485}} {:db/id 17592186483485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231576 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8588f05c-f259-5f6f-95a4-ba743efb8633" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None" :db/id 17592186230323} {:answer/id #uuid "87e2a5ac-5e6b-5176-ada3-76165f3827b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186230324} {:answer/id #uuid "bd0f684b-31be-53dd-959a-4c693200fbd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186230325} {:answer/id #uuid "ebbe1595-b0a0-5005-89d3-b1a66671386d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186230326} {:answer/id #uuid "6ad71e63-ab40-5319-b40d-20fec2c9d4de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186230327}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186230326} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6c1fc5b-ecb6-509b-ab8e-ba64d464ed59" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186230322}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a2dc0571-7d63-58c4-a7e9-b264e1dac3a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-343760" :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. "q-343746" :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =4$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[16(D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-16(C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)]+16t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 16D\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-16C\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=0$ and $D=\frac{5}{8}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Only solution II matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"."} :step/id #uuid "65d89567-4925-56ab-9bcd-c0152afe9d34" :step/next {:db/id 17592186483485}} {:db/id 17592186483460 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231570 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "498bed50-28c7-50fa-a5df-0080495261c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186441791}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186441791} :answer-field/id #uuid "5abd7c36-14a4-56ef-ada9-6c206b80a9d0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186230295}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "968f331f-040e-5a16-a459-23a91c08dfd4" :question/math-academy-id "q-343473" :question/problem "A particle of mass $0.5\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. $$

$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky+(3{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=3(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-1).

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=3(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-1)$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$ Since

$$
f(t)=3(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-1)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),

{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$

$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.8{y}^{″}=-ky+(4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-2).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{4}y=\frac{5}{2}(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-1).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{4}\,⟹\,k=\frac{4}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

$$
f(t)=\frac{5}{2}(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-1)=\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $5.$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{4}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{4}{5}\cdot {5}^{2}=20\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.

The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{3}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{3}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{5}{3}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(6D-9Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-(6C+9Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 6D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-6C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=0$ and $D=\frac{5}{3}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{5}{3}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{3}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{3}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{5}{3}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."} :step/id #uuid "d88d67e5-0c3f-5914-b3bd-6949d7868fd1"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f8deee66-8faa-5103-9ffb-a0528de31c35" $$
y'' + 5y' + 6y = 0,
$$

is given by

$$
y = Ae^{-2x} + Be^{-3x}
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants.

Now, let's consider the same ODE with some additional conditions imposed:

$$
y'' + 5y' + 6y = 0, \quad y(0) = 1, \quad y'(0) = 1.
$$

This is called an **initial value problem (IVP)**. In addition to the differential equation, we are given two **initial conditions**:

$$
y(0) = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad y'(0) = 1.
$$

The goal of an IVP is to use these initial conditions to find specific values for the arbitrary constants $A$ and $B,$ which gives us a unique *particular solution*.

17592186153297 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153337 :tutorial/content "Let's find the particular solution for the **initial value problem**:

$$
y'' + 5y' + 6y =0, \ \ y(0) = 1, \ \ y' (0) = 1.
$$

We start with the general solution:

$$
y(x) = Ae^{-2x} + Be^{-3x}.
$$

**Step 1: Apply the first initial condition, $y(0)=1.$**
Substituting $x=0$ and $y=1$ into the general solution gives our first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A{e}^{-2(0)}+B{e}^{-3(0)} \\ 1 & =A{e}^{0}+B{e}^{0} \\ 1 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2: Apply the second initial condition, $y'(0)=1.$**
First, we need to find the derivative, $y'(x){:}$

$$
y'(x) =  -2 A e ^ { -2 x}  -3 B e ^ {-3 x}.
$$

Now, substituting $x=0$ and $y'=1$ gives our second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-2A{e}^{-2(0)}-3B{e}^{-3(0)} \\ 1 & =-2A{e}^{0}-3B{e}^{0} \\ 1 & =-2A-3B.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Solve the system of equations for $A$ and $B.$**
We have a system of two linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=A+B \\ 1 &=-2A-3B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we can write $A=1-B.$ Substituting this into the second equation:

$$

$$

$$

has the general solution

$$
{y}^{″}+6{y}^{′}+13y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-4.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$

$$

$$
-3P+2Q=-4.
$$

$$
y={e}^{-3x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "175938d0-fece-5a13-994e-7f2a8a04c450" :step/next {:db/id 17592186476986}} {:db/id 17592186476986 :step/content {:db/id 17592186476916 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "501007c1-1237-54a3-8146-49746a54174b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=4{e}^{x}-4x{e}^{x}" :db/id 17592186476368} {:answer/id #uuid "6133a790-bf37-5624-a5e5-d93d8aac76a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=4{e}^{x}+x{e}^{x}" :db/id 17592186476424} {:answer/id #uuid "90703a07-a49f-5b3e-9f80-5fb5897a85ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=4{e}^{x}+2x{e}^{x}" :db/id 17592186476512} {:answer/id #uuid "e78a3592-edab-5dca-829b-212313e22fe6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=4{e}^{x}+4x{e}^{x}" :db/id 17592186476720} {:answer/id #uuid "f6418223-cfc1-5b18-8627-68adb9ed9afd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=4{e}^{x}+8x{e}^{x}" :db/id 17592186476746}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186476720} :answer-field/id #uuid "ca796d4b-8681-5245-bc1d-c35792d5e364" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186476844}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7e57d61a-2fa5-55d2-aed6-295e67c97f51" :question/math-academy-id "q-130350" :question/problem "Given that the differential equation

:question/math-academy-id "q-130374" :question/problem "Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-2.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=2.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-{e}^{-x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{e}^{-x}(-P\operatorname{sin}⁡x+Q\operatorname{cos}⁡x).
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=-2$ into the above to get

$$
-P+Q=-2.
$$

Using the fact that $P=2$ gives $Q=0.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6b359008-56cc-5644-a2dc-31e108447e77"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "505e2df8-db79-59e7-a583-99babc506741" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.$

Let's extract all possible information from this fact using the vector spaces related to the matrix, namely, the *column space* and the *null space*.

- The fact that the unique solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ is $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ tells us that 

$$
\textrm{Null}(A)=\{ \mathbf{0} \},
$$

 or alternatively, 

$$
\textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{nullity}(A)=0.
$$

- Furthermore, if $\textrm{dim(Null}(A))=0$ then $A$ has no *non-pivot* columns, or equivalently, all the columns of $A$ are *pivot columns*. So 

$$
\textrm{dim(Col}(A))=\textrm{rank}(A)=n.
$$

- Finally, since $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its basis has $n$ linearly independent vectors, we can conclude that 

$$
\textrm{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n.
$$

"q-79349" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and  $det(A)=1?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A$ is not invertible

- **II.** $\text{rank}(A)=4$

- **III.** $A$ has $5$ pivot columns" :question/worked-solution "Since $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=5=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

"q-139978" :question/problem "Consider the following sentence:

*If $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $\text{__________}\,.$*

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?

I. $A$ has no inverse

II. $\text{Null}(A)$ has dimension zero

III. $A$ has less than $5$ pivot columns

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=5=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $A$ has no inverse.* $\,✓$ 

Indeed, since $det(A)=0,$ the matrix $A$ can't be invertible.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $\text{Null}(A)$ has dimension zero.* $\,\times $

Since $A$ is not invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\}$ which, in turn,  means that $\text{Null}(A)$ must have a basis so the dimension must be greater than zero.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $A$ has less than $5$ pivot columns.* $\,✓$

Indeed, since $A$ is not invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{dim(Col}(A))\ne 5,$ which means that $A$ has less than $5$ pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "1140fa5b-f47a-5b21-a507-87491673347d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485610}} {:db/id 17592186485604 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125168 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06680c4f-a621-5dc3-875e-3896db2af04b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186460023} {:answer/id #uuid "5c1cf54f-05d3-5550-8f3d-cdfa3137d5bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186460024}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186460023} :answer-field/id #uuid "e3156979-45c5-5d24-80c1-f665fce48ba8" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186460878} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "88c8b9c9-048e-580b-90b5-0615fcacbfe9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186460025} {:answer/id #uuid "5cd76941-0308-57d6-9b7b-3ba6c48171e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186460026}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186460026} :answer-field/id #uuid "44325e4a-3b71-5949-9822-a4ed24085c3a" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186460879} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3989b63d-47f8-5757-bb11-6a685f029eeb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186460027} {:answer/id #uuid "16bc9a89-2517-5c10-b196-866970cad27b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186460028}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186460027} :answer-field/id #uuid "a9665add-7abd-5377-b1f0-9d3eafc436be" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186460880}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7f4e1182-d195-5cca-bb1a-601ea1f9c921" :question/math-academy-id "q-47599" :question/problem "Consider the following sentence:

- **III.** $A$ has $5$ pivot columns
